content: The kit includes a ready-to-use amplification mix containing Taq polymerase. It offers flexibility in DNA extraction, which can be performed manually or automated using the GenoXtract® nucleic acid isolation instrument. Amplification, detection, and evaluation processes can also be automated, making the test suitable for low, medium, and high-throughput settings. This molecular genetic assay is designed to detect the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex and its resistance to rifampicin and/or isoniazid. The GenoType MTBDRplus test operates on the principles of PCR and DNA-STRIP technology. Mycobacterial DNA is extracted from patient specimens or cultured material, amplified via PCR, and detected on a membrane strip using reverse hybridization and an enzymatic color reaction. The manufacturer provides a template to assist users in interpreting the banding patterns on the strips, which are scored visually, transcribed, and reported. In high-volume settings, the automated GenoScan® reader can interpret banding patterns and suggest results, reducing transcription errors. If the operator agrees with the interpretation, results are automatically uploaded. In March 2016, the WHO Global TB Programme convened a Guideline Development Group (GDG) to evaluate the use of the MTBDRsl assay for detecting mutations associated with resistance to fluoroquinolones and second-line injectable drugs (SLIDs) in patients with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB). The GDG reviewed evidence on the diagnostic accuracy and clinical utility of the assay. The test demonstrated high confidence in detecting fluoroquinolone or SLID resistance in MDR/RR-TB patients, whether performed directly on sputum specimens or indirectly on cultured isolates. A positive result provides reliable information for guiding treatment decisions. However, in cases of negative results, phenotypic culture-based drug susceptibility testing (DST) may still be necessary, especially in settings with a high pretest probability of resistance. The use of the MTBDRsl assay in routine care can improve the time to diagnosis of drug resistance, enabling earlier initiation of appropriate therapy and better patient outcomes. The test performs well in direct testing of sputum specimens from confirmed MDR/RR-TB patients, although indeterminate rates are higher for smear-negative specimens compared to smear-positive ones. The GDG recommended using the assay for all sputum specimens from MDR/RR-TB patients, regardless of microscopy results. The SL-LPA test is suitable for use in central or national reference laboratories and can also be implemented at regional levels with appropriate infrastructure. While SL-LPA provides rapid results, it does not eliminate the need for conventional culture and DST capabilities, which remain essential for monitoring treatment response and detecting additional resistance. For pyrazinamide resistance detection, high-complexity reverse hybridization-based nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) may be used on Mycobacterium tuberculosis culture isolates. Pyrazinamide is a key antibiotic for treating both drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB due to its ability to eradicate persistent bacilli and its synergistic properties with other antibiotics. Resistance to pyrazinamide is strongly associated with MDR/RR-TB, with an estimated 30–60% of MDR/RR-TB cases also resistant to pyrazinamide. Detecting pyrazinamide resistance is crucial for clinicians to make informed decisions about including or excluding the drug in treatment regimens. The GenoScholar™ PZA-TB assay, developed by Nipro, is a commercially available line-probe assay (LPA) for detecting pyrazinamide resistance. Unlike other LPAs, it targets a 700-base pair fragment covering the entire pncA gene and promoter region. The assay uses PCR amplification, hybridization to complementary oligonucleotide probes on a membrane strip, and enzymatic color reactions to visually interpret results. The absence of wild-type probe binding indicates the presence of a mutation. While the assay shows promise for routine care, limited data are available on its diagnostic accuracy. The WHO commissioned a systematic review to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of high-complexity reverse hybridization-based NAATs for pyrazinamide resistance detection. The review found insufficient data to draw conclusions about the accuracy of these tests on sputum samples. For isolates, seven studies with 964 participants were analyzed, but the evidence was downgraded due to selection bias, indirectness, and inconsistency. Sensitivity ranged from 36% to 100%, and specificity from 96% to 100%. Cost-effectiveness analyses for the GenoScholar PZA-TB II assay are limited. The test kit costs approximately $16 per test, with equipment priced at $14,000. Operational costs, often higher than test kit costs, vary across settings. While the assay could potentially reduce diagnostic delays and improve treatment outcomes, further research is needed to assess its economic feasibility and impact on health equity. End-user perspectives highlight the importance of rapid, accurate diagnostics and equitable access to testing. Barriers such as diagnostic delays, limited facilities, and eligibility restrictions disproportionately affect vulnerable populations. Stakeholders emphasize the need for sustainable funding, clear communication of diagnostic options, and alignment of new diagnostics with treatment advancements.
